content: This is an updated version of a Cochrane review originally published in 2001. Approximately one-third of individuals with epilepsy experience drug-resistant seizures that are not adequately controlled by current treatments. As a result, there has been ongoing research into new antiepileptic drugs, leveraging advancements in understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying epilepsy and seizures. Calcium antagonists, which can modulate the effects of calcium on neuronal activity, have been explored as potential add-on therapies for drug-resistant epilepsy. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of calcium antagonists when used as adjunctive treatments for individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and SCOPUS, up to January 29, 2013. The inclusion criteria were randomized, placebo-controlled, or active-controlled trials evaluating calcium antagonists as add-on therapies in this population. Two independent reviewers selected eligible studies and extracted data. The outcomes of interest included a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, treatment withdrawal rates, adverse effects, cognitive outcomes, and quality of life. Analyses were performed on an intention-to-treat basis. The review included 11 trials with a total of 424 participants. These trials investigated three calcium antagonists: flunarizine, nimodipine, and nifedipine. Specifically, there was one parallel-group trial and seven cross-over trials evaluating flunarizine, two cross-over trials assessing nimodipine, and one cross-over trial examining nifedipine. For flunarizine, a single parallel-group trial reported a risk ratio (RR) of 1.53 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59 to 3.96) for achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, indicating no statistically significant benefit. Data for this outcome were not available from the other seven cross-over trials. However, the overall RR for treatment withdrawal with flunarizine was 7.11 (95% CI 1.73 to 29.30), suggesting a significantly higher likelihood of treatment discontinuation compared to placebo. No statistically significant adverse effects were associated with flunarizine. For nifedipine, the required data for the specified outcomes were not available. For nimodipine, data were limited to the first treatment period of one cross-over trial involving 17 participants. The RR for achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency was 7.78 (99% CI 0.46 to 130.88), and the RR for treatment withdrawal was 2.25 (99% CI 0.25 to 20.38). These results were inconclusive due to the wide confidence intervals and small sample size. In conclusion, flunarizine may have a minimal effect on reducing seizure frequency but is associated with a significantly higher withdrawal rate, likely due to adverse effects, and therefore should not be recommended as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy. Similarly, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of nifedipine or nimodipine as adjunctive treatments for epilepsy.
